title: Hola: the Nihang parade
hookLine: the Nihang dals ride and display gatka at Anandpur

cards: Hooves on hard ground, and a roar from the crowd. A rider in deep blue leans out of the saddle at a gallop and lifts something from the dirt with the tip of a spear.
Behind him come more riders, tall turbans, flags snapping on long poles, drums. On the edge of the field, two young men circle each other with sticks and small shields, laughing between blows.
This is Anandpur Sahib at Hola Mohalla, and the riders are the Nihang Singhs.

teach.b: This path has met Hola Mohalla, gatka and the Nihangs, each on its own day.
Today, the parade as a day of memory.
The Nihang Singhs are organized in bands called dals, and at Hola they come to Anandpur with their horses, flags and old weapons, and ride in procession through the town and out onto the open ground.
It's a parade, not a war. Tradition says Guru Gobind Singh called the Sikhs together at Anandpur for drills and mock battles, turning the spring season of Holi toward courage.
The Nihangs keep that memory the way it was given: as play with a purpose. The horsemanship is real and the skill hard won, but the mood is a festival, not a threat.
In the dust, pairs spar at gatka with stick and shield, footwork first, eyes on the partner. Children watch and copy.
A skill that could have been lost is passed on in public, in joy.

In the Dasam Granth, in a hymn often sung as Deh Shiva, Guru Gobind Singh asks, in paraphrase, for one boon: that he never turn back from doing good. It's a prayer for courage, and Sikhs sing it at gatherings.
The parade gives that prayer a body: people who ride forward, not back, and do it laughing. Memory doesn't always have to be quiet. Sometimes it gallops.

how: At Hola Mohalla in Anandpur Sahib, Nihang Singh dals ride in procession with horses and flags, display horsemanship and gatka, and the gathering includes kirtan and langar.

o: the spring days of riding and gatka at Anandpur

practice: If you're able, stand and shake out your hands, arms and shoulders, then march in place a few steps with your knees a little high, and let it be a bit silly, smiling if you can.

Take three strong breaths, in through the nose and out through the mouth, then sit and feel your heart going, joy and strength in the same body. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with each breath as it slows.

wordCard.voice: Hola. The spring days at Anandpur Sahib when the Nihang dals ride in procession and gatka is played in public, memory kept in motion. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Nihang, the name of the Sikh order known for blue robes and the old martial ways.

carryVoice: Your line: ride in joy. Deh Shiva asks: never turn back from doing good. See you tomorrow.
